label: Blackwood Manor
title: Rain over Blackwood Manor
premise: Autumn, nineteen twenty-four, in the English countryside. It has rained all day on Blackwood Manor, the old country house of Sir Edmund Blackwood, and the river has already risen over the bridge on the lane. After dinner, between the fires in the grates and the drumming of water on the panes, someone in the house decides that Sir Edmund will not live to see the dawn.

art.style: atmospheric cinematic oil painting, English country-house mystery, 1924, rain-dark windows, muted dark teal and brass palette, warm lamplight, deep soft shadows, realistic proportions

victim.name: Sir Edmund Blackwood
victim.description: Baronet, widower and former colonel in the Great War, master of Blackwood Manor and of the farms around it. A collector of rare plants, exacting about money and given to changing his will with the mood of the week, he ruled family and servants alike with icy courtesy and a merciless memory for other people's failings.

people.name: Elena Blackwood
people.personality: Sir Edmund's only child, motherless since girlhood and raised by her father to inherit the house. Proud, restrained and entirely self-possessed. Cool and formal, never familiar; speaks in complete, firm sentences, seeks no sympathy and never apologises. Under pressure she demands precision, and never raises her voice or stoops to insult. Says ‘let me be perfectly clear’ and ‘don't twist my words’, and cuts any insinuation dead.
people.appearance: A woman of nearly thirty, tall and upright, with a pale face and high cheekbones. Grey-green eyes, fine brows and lips with scarcely any colour. Her dark hair is cut in a sleek shingle. She wears a black velvet drop-waist dress, a long string of jet beads and a grey silk shawl about her shoulders.

rooms.name: Study
rooms.description: Dark oak panelling, a mahogany desk with a green leather top and a brass lamp that leaves the rest of the room in half-light. It smells of pipe tobacco and ink, and the rain beats ceaselessly on the closed windows.
ambience: As you enter, you feel the chill of the dead fireplace and hear the tick of a mantel clock nobody has looked at in hours. The leather armchairs creak at the slightest movement.
The brass lamp casts a green circle on the desk top and leaves the rest in shadow. The windows shudder at every gust, and the smell of stale tobacco clings to your clothes.

arrivals: The hired car crawls along a lane turned to mud, its headlamps lost in the curtain of rain. At the end of the oak avenue Blackwood Manor appears, dark but for a few lit windows. Someone waits for you on the front steps beneath a black umbrella.

You step off the last train at a village station with a single lamp and a flooded platform. A car from the house carries you between sodden hedges to the iron gates of Blackwood Manor. When the engine stops, only the sound of the rain remains.

The telephone call dragged you from your London flat at an ungodly hour, the line all crackle and a voice asking for discretion. Now you step through the door of Blackwood Manor, your coat dripping onto the marble. It smells of woodsmoke, wax and wet earth.

You were passing through on your way north when the swollen river cut the road, and the only lit house for miles around is Blackwood Manor. You knock, hat pulled low and water running down your collar. The door opens before the second knock.
tensions: The bridge is under water and the storm has brought down the telephone line. Nobody will leave Blackwood Manor before dawn, and whoever did it knows that as well as you do.
By the fireplace, several faces watch you in the lamplight without a word. They have all known one another for years, and at least one of them is lying.
You ask for paper, a pen and a strong pot of coffee. The hall clock goes on striking the quarters: before the rain lets up, you must sort the alibis from the lies.

night: The rain beats harder against the panes and the wind begins to whistle in the chimneys. In the hall, the longcase clock goes on striking the quarters, unhurried.
In the kitchen someone puts the kettle on again; nobody in the house means to go to bed. Footsteps in the corridors stop, then move away again.
A long roll of thunder rumbles over the countryside and the lamps flicker for an instant. The maids hand out candles along the passages, in case the lights fail.
The river keeps rising: from the upper windows the water can be seen gleaming where the meadow used to be. Nobody mentions the bridge any more.
The candles have burned down to stubs and the house smells of cold smoke. Upstairs, a door closes far too softly.
The storm is at its worst: shutters bang and the fires shrink in the grates. Everyone waits, and nobody dares look at the others.
epilogues: When you finish speaking, the silence is so deep you can hear the umbrellas dripping in the hall. Nobody looks at {culprit}. The housekeeper crosses the room without a sound and comes to stand alongside, firm as a sentry, while someone closes the door of {scene}. {culprit} offers no resistance and sits down on a step of the oak staircase to wait. Towards dawn the rain eases, the river slowly draws back from the bridge and, with the first grey light, the county police car appears along the oak avenue.

{culprit} hears the accusation without interrupting. At the end there is only a request for a glass of water, and it is the housekeeper who brings it, without a word, on the silver tray kept for great occasions. {culprit}'s hands shake taking it. Nobody else moves. There is not a whole candle left in the house when, shortly before dawn, the cocks on the farms begin to crow and the water stops beating on the panes. By mid-morning the village sergeant crosses the bridge in muddy boots and leads {culprit} away down the oak avenue.

You have left the question that mattered until last, and {culprit}'s answer is a long silence. The housekeeper, who has stood by the door all night, is the first to understand: she sighs and orders that nobody is to leave the house. They lock {culprit} in the silver room, the only one with a bolt on the outside, and {victim} is laid out in {scene} beneath a linen sheet. At dawn the rain finally stops. A pale sun rises over the flooded meadows, and from the window you watch the county inspector arrive, splashing through the puddles.
